newsitem.title: UK: ERM threat unlikely to be used to cap stg-analysts.
newsitem.headline: ERM threat unlikely to be used to cap stg-analysts.

text.p: Official hints of an eventual British return to Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM) may be one of the only ways left to rein in rampant sterling but few analysts believe such a threat is credible in the near term.
The new British Labour government may be more open to the prospect of European monetary union further down the line, they said.
But the sharp contrast in economic cycles between Britain and continental Europe right now would render exchange rate targeting as hazardous as it was the last time around.

"I doubt there is any appetite in the current government for using the exchange rate to converge on a Europe with high unemployment and structural economic problems," said Joe Prendergast, head of currency research and strategy at CSFB.
"EMU may become a factor in the years ahead but there's no rush here. Sterling strength is reflecting a strong economy and I don't see the major policy problem with that."
Sterling's 30 percent surge against the mark over the past year is making exporters wince and the government has publicly stated it is concerned.
Rumours in early May that Labour advisers favoured ERM re-entry at a peg to the mark as low as 2.50 acted as a drag on the pound for weeks. The rumours were strenuously denied.
The pound's rise to its old ERM central parity at 2.95 marks this week brought Britain's two-year membership of the system from 1990 to 1992 back to mind.

Sterling was forced out of the ERM by a wave of speculation in September 1992 as traders bet that interest rate levels appropriate for an overheating German economy were not compatible with a deepening British recession.

"When sterling was last at 2.95 marks the German economy was growing at 6.8 percent and the UK was contracting at about 2.8 percent. Clearly there was a problem keeping the exchange rate stable," said Michael Burke, economist at Citibank.
"The differences in the relative business cycles makes it a far more comfortable place to be this time around and justified despite fair value estimates."
In the past 18 months, the pound has more than recovered the losses of about 20 percent suffered after leaving the ERM. The economic tables have turned, too.

This week, Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's failure to tighten fiscal policy enough in his 1997/98 budget means the market is now betting aggressively on further interest rate rises to dampen consumer demand. This is making the pound's high-yield magnet even more attractive.
Against that background, there is very little the authorities can do in practical terms to cap the pound, analysts said.
Traders say central bank intervention would only be a temporary barrier if interest rates are being raised at the same time. The ERM threat, too, lacks credibility at this stage.

"Even if they did (hint at ERM re-entry), it wouldn't have too much impact on the pound. It could cause a short-term panic in the market but it's difficult to see sterling/mark suffering too much," John Meisner, head of spot foreign exchange at Standard Chartered, said.

Burke at Citibank also said that even if ERM reentry were mooted, there was no guarantee the rest of the EU would allow the pound to be fixed at a much lower rate than at present and, as a result, the impact could be limited.

One way of glimpsing at how sterling might trade in the ERM is to look at the Irish punt. Like its larger neighbour, the Irish economy is booming but the punt is in the ERM and aspires to be in at the start of European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.

The currency is causing policy strains. It is trading in the ERM grid almost 11 percent above the weakest placed French franc, compared with a maximum allowed fluctuation of 15 percent. It has weakened against sterling in the meantime.

Analysts said the punt's weakness against sterling was exaggerating inflationary pressures and these pressures, in turn, were preventing the central bank from cutting interest rates to cap the punt in its ERM bands.

"The UK government is not concerned about the pound to the extent of taking such a radical step as ERM membership," said Prendergast at CSFB. "If they really wanted to do something about the pound, they would have done so in the budget."
